sections.name: Performance Optimization Fundamentals
sections.explanation_simple: Game optimization is about making your game run smoothly on its target hardware. A game running at 30fps has only 33 milliseconds to do EVERYTHING per frame: process input, update AI, run physics, and draw everything. Optimization is about spending those milliseconds wisely. The golden rule is: FIND THE BOTTLENECK FIRST. Don't optimize randomly - use profilers to find what's actually slow. 90% of the time, the slow part is one or two systems, and fixing those gives you 90% of the performance gain.
key_concepts: Bottleneck: The slowest part of your frame (CPU, GPU, or memory bound)
Draw Call: Command to GPU to render something (keep under 2000 on console, 100 on mobile)
Frame Budget: Total time per frame (16.6ms for 60fps, 33.3ms for 30fps)
CPU Bound: Game logic/AI/physics is the bottleneck
GPU Bound: Rendering is the bottleneck
Fill Rate: How many pixels GPU can fill per second
Overdraw: Drawing the same pixel multiple times (transparency kills)
Cache Miss: CPU waiting for data from RAM (bigger problem than you think)
Memory Bandwidth: How fast data can move between RAM and GPU
Garbage Collection: Automatic memory cleanup (can cause frame stutters!)
Batching: Combining multiple draw calls into one
Instancing: Drawing many copies of the same mesh in one call
Occlusion Culling: Not rendering objects hidden behind walls
Level Streaming: Loading/unloading parts of the world as player moves

sections.name: Console & Platform Development
sections.explanation_simple: Making a game for consoles (PlayStation, Xbox, Nintendo Switch) is very different from making a PC game. Consoles have FIXED hardware - every PS5 has the same GPU, CPU, and RAM. This means you can optimize specifically for that hardware, but it also means you have strict limits. Console SDKs (Software Development Kits) from Sony, Microsoft, and Nintendo come with specific rules: no accessing the file system freely, no dynamic linking, specific controller APIs, and certification requirements (the game must pass their tests before release). VR adds even more rules: you MUST maintain 90fps or players get motion sick.
key_concepts: NDA: Console SDKs require signing non-disclosure agreements
Development Kit (Dev Kit): Special console hardware for development
Certification (TRC/XR): Console manufacturer's testing requirements
PS5: Custom SSD architecture, Tempest Engine (3D audio), DualSense features
Xbox Series X/S: GDK (Game Development Kit), Xbox Velocity Architecture
Nintendo Switch: Lower power, unique dual-mode (docked/portable), ARM CPU
VR: 90fps minimum requirement, async timewarp, foveated rendering
Steam: No cert requirements but extensive API (achievements, cloud saves, multiplayer)
Epic Games Store: Revenue share terms, account services
Mobile: Fragmentation (thousands of Android devices), thermal throttling
Cross-Platform: Building the same game for multiple platforms with shared code

code_examples.title: Cross-Platform Build System (CMake)
code_examples.code:
# CMakeLists.txt - Build for multiple platforms
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(MyGame)

# Platform detection
if(WIN32)
    add_definitions(-DPLATFORM_WINDOWS)
    set(PLATFORM_SOURCES
        src/Platform/Windows/Window_Win32.cpp
        src/Platform/Windows/Input_Win32.cpp
    )
elseif(APPLE)
    add_definitions(-DPLATFORM_MACOS)
    set(PLATFORM_SOURCES
        src/Platform/MacOS/Window_MacOS.mm
        src/Platform/MacOS/Input_MacOS.mm
    )
elseif(ANDROID)
    add_definitions(-DPLATFORM_ANDROID)
    set(PLATFORM_SOURCES
        src/Platform/Android/Window_Android.cpp
        src/Platform/Android/Input_Android.cpp
    )
endif()

# Renderer selection
option(USE_VULKAN "Use Vulkan renderer" ON)
option(USE_DX12 "Use DirectX 12 renderer" OFF)

if(USE_VULKAN)
    add_definitions(-DUSE_VULKAN)
    find_package(Vulkan REQUIRED)
endif()

# Game code (platform-independent)
add_library(GameCore STATIC
    src/Game/GameLoop.cpp
    src/Game/Entity.cpp
    src/Game/Physics.cpp
    src/Game/Renderer.cpp
    ${PLATFORM_SOURCES}
)

# Platform-specific executables
if(WIN32)
    add_executable(MyGame_Win32 main.cpp)
    target_link_libraries(MyGame_Win32 GameCore)
elseif(APPLE)
    add_executable(MyGame_Mac main.cpp)
    target_link_libraries(MyGame_Mac GameCore)
endif()

sections.name: AAA Specializations: Digital Humans, Photogrammetry & Virtual Production
sections.explanation_simple: AAA games use Hollywood-level techniques to create realistic characters and worlds. Digital humans (like MetaHuman from Epic Games) create photorealistic people that you can't tell are CGI. Photogrammetry is taking hundreds of photos of real objects and converting them into 3D models - this is how games like The Last of Us Part 2 create incredibly realistic environments. Virtual production uses real-time game engines to make movies (The Mandalorian uses Unreal Engine with giant LED walls). These techniques blur the line between game development and filmmaking.
key_concepts: MetaHuman: Epic's free digital human system - creates realistic characters in minutes
Photogrammetry: Taking photos from multiple angles to create 3D models from real life
RealityCapture: Industry standard photogrammetry software (fast, high quality)
Agisoft Metashape: Alternative photogrammetry tool (easier to learn)
Virtual Production: Using game engine for real-time filmmaking (The Mandalorian, 1899)
LED Volume: Giant curved LED screen that shows the virtual background (replaces green screen)
Camera Tracking: Tracking camera position in real-time so perspective matches the scene
Digital Twin: A virtual copy of a real location (for film/game use)
Facial Capture: Recording actor's face with helmet camera for realistic expressions
Procedural Cities: Houdini + UE5 generating entire cities (like Spider-Man's NYC)
Military Simulation: Games used for training (VBS4, Steel Beasts)
Streaming Infrastructure: How massive open worlds stream in content as you move

code_examples.title: Photogrammetry Pipeline
code_examples.code:
# ===== COMPLETE PHOTOGRAMMETRY WORKFLOW =====

"""
STEP 1: CAPTURE
  - Camera: DSLR or high-end phone (iPhone 14 Pro or better)
  - Settings: Manual mode, fixed aperture, fixed ISO, RAW format
  - Subject: 30-50% overlap between adjacent photos
  - Coverage: Photograph from ALL angles (top, bottom, sides)
  - Lighting: Even, diffused lighting (cloudy day or studio lights)
  - Calibration: Include a scale reference object

STEP 2: PROCESSING (RealityCapture)
  1. Import photos
  2. Align images (calculate camera positions)
  3. Create dense point cloud
  4. Build mesh (high polygon)
  5. Create texture (unwrap UVs, bake color from photos)
  6. Export as FBX/OBJ with textures

STEP 3: OPTIMIZATION FOR GAMES
  1. Decimate mesh (reduce polygons: 10M -> 50K)
  2. Retopologize (create clean edge flow)
  3. Bake normal map from high-poly to low-poly
  4. Bake ambient occlusion map
  5. Create LODs
  6. Import to game engine
"""

# RealityCapture command line (batch processing):
# rc --input "D:\scans\statue\photos" --align --quality medium --output "D:\scans\statue\output"

# ===== MEGASCANS: The easy way =====
# Quixel Megascans and Epic Games provide
# thousands of ready-to-use photogrammetry assets
# for free in Unreal Engine

# ===== METAHUMAN SETUP =====
# 1. Go to metahuman.unrealengine.com
# 2. Create a face by morphing presets (or use MetaHuman Animator from iPhone scan)
# 3. Customize: hair, skin, eyes, clothing
# 4. Export to your Unreal project
# 5. Character comes fully rigged, with LODs, with facial controls
# 6. Use with LiveLink Face app for real-time facial mocap

// MetaHuman C++ control in Unreal:
void AMyGameMode::SpawnMetaHumanCharacter()
{
    // MetaHuman is just a Character blueprint
    ACharacter* MH = GetWorld()->SpawnActor<ACharacter>(
        MetaHumanClass,
        SpawnLocation,
        SpawnRotation
    );

    // Facial animation through LiveLink
    if (LiveLinkComponent)
    {
        LiveLinkComponent->SetSubjectName(FName("FaceCapture"));
        LiveLinkComponent->Initialize();
    }
}

sections.name: Reverse Engineering, Modding & Game Security
sections.explanation_simple: Reverse engineering is taking something apart to understand how it works - like a watchmaker who disassembles a watch to see how all the gears fit together. In games, this means analyzing compiled game code to understand how systems work. Modding is modifying games to add new content, fix bugs, or change gameplay. Game security is about preventing cheating and protecting the game from tampering. Understanding all three makes you a better game developer because you understand how games REALLY work under the hood.
key_concepts: Binary Analysis: Reading compiled machine code (assembly) to understand the program
Disassembler: Tool that converts machine code to assembly (IDA Pro, Ghidra, x64dbg)
Memory Editing: Changing values in RAM (health, ammo, position) while game runs (Cheat Engine)
Detour/Hook: Intercepting function calls to modify behavior
DLL Injection: Injecting custom code into a running game process
Mod SDK: Official tools provided by game developers for creating mods
Plugin Architecture: Allowing third-party code to extend the game
Anti-Cheat: Systems that detect tampering (Easy Anti-Cheat, BattlEye, VAC)
Server Authority: Server makes final decisions, client can't override (prevents cheating)
Obfuscation: Making code hard to read by reverse engineers
Encryption: Protecting game assets and network traffic
Cheat Detection: Analyzing player behavior patterns for anomalies
